contentHtml:
With employer-provided health cover often ending at retirement, India’s sixty-somethings face a significant healthcare coverage gap. Pavan Choudary, Chairman, Medical Technology Association of India, highlights the need to bridge this gap through wider insurance coverage, preventive care and early intervention

Sixty should be an age of new beginnings, not growing anxieties about healthcare. After decades of work, raising families and contributing to society, retirement should offer the freedom to live life on one’s own terms. Yet, for millions of Indians, it also marks the loss of employer-provided health insurance, just as the need for medical care begins to grow.

India has taken a commendable step by extending Ayushman Bharat coverage to all citizens aged 70 and above. But what happens in the decade before seventy? These are often the years when timely medical attention can prevent manageable conditions from becoming life altering illnesses. The real challenge is not simply adding years to life, but ensuring those years are lived in good health and dignity.

A demographic arriving early

India’s elderly population is growing faster than the nation as a whole. The UNFPA’s India Ageing Report 2023 estimated about 149 million people aged 60 and above in 2022, roughly 10.5 per cent of the population, and projects this to reach 347 million, or 20.8 per cent, by 2050. The decadal growth rate of the elderly is about 41 per cent, and by 2046 older Indians are likely to outnumber children aged 0 to 15. According to the UNFPA 2023 report, more than 40 per cent of the elderly belong to the poorest wealth quintile, and about 18.7 per cent have no income at all.

These are not distant numbers. The person who will turn seventy in 2036 is sixty today, and is deciding right now whether that persistent breathlessness on the stairs is worth a doctor’s fee.

The decade that policy forgot

In September 2024, the Union Cabinet extended Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY to every citizen aged 70 and above, irrespective of income. The Ayushman Vaya Vandana scheme was rolled out on 29 October 2024 for about six crore senior citizens in 4.5 crore families. By September 2026, more than 1.36 crore schemes had been issued. This is a genuinely historic step, and it deserves full credit.

Yet it leaves a conspicuous gap. For most salaried Indians, employer-provided health cover ends at retirement, at 58 or 60. Private insurance must then be bought at the steepest point of the premium curve, often with waiting periods for precisely the conditions that have just surfaced. The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India found that only 18.2 per cent of people aged 60 and above had any health insurance. Unless they are poor enough to qualify for PM-JAY’s family-based eligibility, many sixty-somethings face a ten-year wait for state-backed cover during the very years their bodies begin to send bills.

The regulator has helped at the margins. IRDAI removed the 65-year upper age limit for buying health insurance from April 2024 and, in January 2025, capped annual premium increases for policyholders aged 60 and above at 10 per cent unless it gives prior approval. Parliament has noticed too. In March 2025, the Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare recommended that the age criterion for Vaya Vandana schemes be rationalised to 60 years and that cover be raised from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh.

The economics of early intervention

Here lies the insight that policymakers should seize: the sixties are the decade of maximum leverage. A 62-year-old whose blood pressure is detected and controlled is far less likely to become the stroke patient of 72, whose care Vaya Vandana will then fund at many times the cost and with far poorer outcomes. Covering the seventies but not the sixties is like insuring a house against fire while declining to pay for smoke detectors.

Vision offers the clearest example. The National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey 2015-19 found that cataract causes 66.2 per cent of blindness among Indians aged 50 and above, and that around 93 per cent of such blindness is avoidable. A routine cataract operation often takes less than half an hour. The same logic applies to hearing aids that keep people socially and economically engaged, and to joint replacements that restore mobility, injuries that in older people frequently mark the end of independent life.

A six-point bridge for the forgotten decade

First, phase Vaya Vandana scheme down to sixty.

Second, pay for prevention, not just hospitalisation. Inpatient-only cover, in effect, rewards illness. India should introduce a “Welcome to Sixty” health check, similar to the “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit that the United States offers once in the first year of Medicare Part B, covering blood pressure, blood sugar, vision, hearing, bone health, mood and fall risk. The delivery platforms already exist: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs have recorded over 540 crore footfalls and e-Sanjeevani more than 50 crore teleconsultations.

Third, value the technologies that preserve independence. Intraocular lenses, hearing aids, orthopaedic implants, home monitoring devices and mobility aids are not luxuries; they are the infrastructure of healthy ageing. Procurement and pricing should be guided by health technology assessment that weighs outcomes across a patient’s remaining years, not merely the lowest upfront price. An implant that is cheaper today but fails sooner is no saving, for the patient or for the payer.

Fourth, build geriatric capacity at the front line. The National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly, launched in 2010-11, envisaged dedicated geriatric services from district hospitals down to sub-centres. Rather than wait for scarce specialists, India should train community health officers and family physicians in the essentials of geriatric assessment, medication review and falls screening.

Fifth, let the record travel with the patient. With more than 97 crore ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) IDs created, India has something few countries possess: the means to keep a continuous digital health record from the sixties into the seventies, so that a diagnosis made at 61 informs the care given at 71.

Sixth, the health cover should be raised from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh.

Respect is a health policy

Our civilisation has always spoken of its elders with reverence. But reverence that stops at the clinic door is sentiment, not policy. The test of a health system is not only how it treats the very old and the very sick, but whether it helps people avoid becoming very sick in the first place.

India has done the hard part. It has built schemes, digital platforms and hospital networks that now reach hundreds of millions. What remains is to close the ten-year gap between retirement and entitlement. The sixties are not the waiting room of old age; they are its foundation. Build that foundation well, and the seventies will cost the nation less while giving its citizens more.
